system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 4 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2174-01-04 11:53:00 to 2174-01-07 13:00:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted for chronic G-tube site pain due to mechanical pulling of the tube, which failed to resolve with prior interventions. She underwent an open gastrostomy tube replacement without complications. Postoperatively, she remained stable, afebrile, and alert, with good pain control managed initially with PCA and transitioned to oral Dilaudid via G-tube. Tube feeds were restarted on postoperative day 2 and advanced to her prior rate of 65 mL/hour, which she tolerated well. She resumed sipping water, ambulated early, and had no signs of infection or bleeding. A MRSA screen was negative. She was discharged home with home health services for wound care, instructions to crush all medications and administer via G-tube, and clear guidance on activity restrictions, diet, and warning signs. Follow-up was arranged with her surgeon.
problems: Other specified procedures as the cause of abnormal reaction of patient, or of later complication, without mention of misadventure at time of procedure

radiology_notes.text:
EXAMINATION:  CT ABD AND PELVIS WITH CONTRAST

INDICATION:  ___ with Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, possible efferent limb
obstruction, Gtube in place.  Please eval for efferent limb obstruction - no
PO contrast but contrast through G-tube and IV contrast (requested by
bariatrics fellow).

TECHNIQUE:  MDCT axial images were acquired through the abdomen and pelvis
following intravenous contrast administration with split bolus technique.
Coronal and sagittal reformations were performed and reviewed on PACS.
Enteric contrast was not administered through the G-tube.  After the study was
completed, Dr. ___ spoke with the ED resident Dr. ___ to give this
report.  Dr. ___ spoke with the bariatrics fellow, who stated repeat
scanning with oral contrast was not necessary.

DOSE:  Total DLP (Body) = 901 mGy-cm.
IV Contrast:  130 mL Omnipaque

COMPARISON:  CT abdomen pelvis from ___ and ___.

FINDINGS: 

LOWER CHEST: There is bibasilar atelectasis but no pleural effusion or
pericardial effusion.

ABDOMEN:

HEPATOBILIARY: The liver demonstrates homogenous attenuation throughout. 
There is no evidence of focal lesions. There is no evidence of intrahepatic or
extrahepatic biliary dilatation. The gallbladder is unremarkable.

PANCREAS: The pancreas has normal attenuation throughout, without evidence of
focal lesions or pancreatic ductal dilatation.  There is no peripancreatic
stranding.

SPLEEN: The spleen shows normal size and attenuation throughout, without
evidence of focal lesions.

ADRENALS: The right and left adrenal glands are normal in size and shape.

URINARY: Duplex kidneys seen bilaterally with two ureters seen proximally
bilaterally.  On the left, these ureters fuse in the pelvis before the level
of the UVJ.  It is unclear if and where they fuse on the right.  The kidneys
are of normal and symmetric size with normal nephrogram.  There are no focal
renal lesions or hydronephrosis. There is no perinephric abnormality.

GASTROINTESTINAL: Patient is post Roux-en-Y gastric bypass.  The G-tube, with
distended balloon, is unchanged in position and located in the excluded
portion of the stomach.  There is no evidence of bowel loop dilation or
evidence of obstruction. Colon and rectum are within normal limits.  The
appendix is not identified, but there are no secondary findings of
appendicitis.  There is no evidence of mesenteric lymphadenopathy.

RETROPERITONEUM: There is no evidence of retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy.

VASCULAR: There is no abdominal aortic aneurysm. There is no calcium burden in
the abdominal aorta and great abdominal arteries.

PELVIS: The urinary bladder and distal ureters are unremarkable. There is no
evidence of pelvic or inguinal lymphadenopathy. There is no free fluid in the
pelvis.

REPRODUCTIVE ORGANS: Reproductive organs are within normal limits.

BONES AND SOFT TISSUES: There is no evidence of worrisome osseous lesions.
Superior to the umbilicus, there is a midline abdominal incision with packing
material (2:26).  No soft tissue fat stranding is identified around this
incision.

IMPRESSION: 

1.  Post Roux-en-Y gastric bypass without evidence of small bowel loop
obstruction.  G-tube is unchanged in position in the excluded portion of the
stomach.

2.  Midline abdominal incision with overlying and indwelling packing material,
per exam by Dr. ___.  No adjacent fat stranding in this region.

NOTIFICATION:  The above findings were communicated via telephone by Dr.
___ to Dr. ___ at the time of the scan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you've been having abdominal pain. Can you tell me more about it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s on the right side, near my belly and lower abdomen. It started about four days ago and hurts more when I move.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Is it constant or does it come and go? And how would you rate the pain, on a scale from 1 to 10?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It was an 8 at first, but now it’s around a 5. Lying still helps a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. You mentioned nausea too. Has that gotten worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, it’s about the same. I still take Zofran in the morning like usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ve reviewed your history. You’ve had gastric bypass and now rely on tube feeds, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. After the surgery, I couldn’t keep food down, so I’ve been on tube feeds for a while.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve stopped your tube feeds for now and started IV fluids to let your gut rest. We also ordered a CT scan to check for any blockages.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is there a chance something’s blocked? I’ve been worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s possible, but your symptoms could also be from irritation or bacterial overgrowth. The CT will help us rule out a blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. And my G-tube is still working fine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the tube is in place and the site looks clean. We’ll keep monitoring it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your CT scan is back. Good news — no signs of a blockage in your intestines. The G-tube is where it should be, in the excluded stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. So what’s causing the pain then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think it’s likely due to irritation from the tube feeds or possibly bacterial overgrowth, which you’ve had before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on rifaximin for that. Should we keep it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll continue your rifaximin. We’ll also start adding back your tube feeds slowly tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, but what if the pain comes back when we restart them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start very low and go slow. If you have any issues, we’ll pause and reassess. Your safety comes first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s the pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s better, maybe a 3 now. I slept okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’re going to start your tube feeds again at a low rate — 20 cc per hour — and increase slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And what about my nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep your morning Zofran. Let us know if it gets worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve started your tube feeds at 20 cc/hr. The nurse will monitor you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel a little full, but no pain yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The enteral nutrition team just confirmed your feeds are infusing well at 20 cc/hr. No issues so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Can we go higher later?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We’ll assess this afternoon. We don’t want to rush it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs came back — all stable. White count is normal, no signs of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my liver and kidneys? I’ve had fatty liver before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Liver enzymes are normal. Kidney function is excellent. You’re doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pain is down to a 2. Feels like I’m turning a corner.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. We’ve increased your tube feeds to 40 cc/hr and plan to go to 60 by tonight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s my usual rate. I hope I can stay on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re optimistic. We’re also adding sucralfate to protect your stomach lining and lansoprazole for acid control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that because of my past ulcers?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It’s preventive. We also added docusate for constipation, which can happen with pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been on 60 cc/hr for a few hours and tolerating it well. We’re calling that a success.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Does this mean I can go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly tomorrow. We’ll make sure your pain is controlled and you’re stable on full feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll need help with wound care, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, home health will visit to help with dressing changes. We’ll set that up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news — you’re being discharged today. Pain is well-controlled, and you’re on full tube feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What meds am I going home with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Rifaximin twice daily, sucralfate three times a day, lansoprazole twice daily, docusate twice daily, and Dilaudid for pain as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And when should I call or come back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you have a fever over 101.5, severe pain, vomiting, or redness around the tube site, come back right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thank you for taking such good care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll follow up with your surgeon for an appointment. Rest well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming — home health is set for wound care, and your pharmacy has your prescriptions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I got the call. Everything’s arranged.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’re cleared to go home. Take care and keep in touch.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I really appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing — make sure to crush all pills before giving them through the G-tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I remember from last time. I’ll be careful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. And avoid heavy lifting for now. Let the incision heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Understood. I’ll take it easy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re officially discharged. Home health will visit tomorrow. Call us with any concerns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad. Take care and rest well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just wanted to say I made it home safely. Everything’s set up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s wonderful to hear. We’ll check in soon. Rest and recover.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted for right-sided abdominal pain and nausea, occurring four days prior to admission. She has a history of gastric bypass and relies on tube feeds due to poor oral intake and post-surgical hypoglycemia. Initial management included NPO status and IV fluids. A CT scan ruled out bowel obstruction, showing the G-tube in correct position without signs of blockage. Tube feeds were restarted gradually and advanced to her baseline rate of 60 cc/hr, which she tolerated well. Pain and nausea were controlled throughout the stay. She was discharged home with home health services for wound care, continuing rifaximin, sucralfate, lansoprazole, docusate, and PRN Dilaudid. Follow-up was arranged with her surgeon.
